She does not emphasize unnecessary memorization for things like super specific pKa values or complicated mechanisms or nomenclature. She makes the course manageable.

Things about the class I liked: Hirschauer provides a practice problem set ranging from easy to difficult for every single chapter we go through as well as talked-through explanations. These are SO helpful, make sure to do them. Some of the more difficult problems definitely reflect what's on the exam. Make sure you're able to actually understand what you're doing for all of them. She gives you a homework category worth 10% with 8 attempts each, basically allowing you to continue to try until you have a full understanding of the content. It's meant to help you learn, not reduce your grade, and you can go to her and ask her for help on anything you genuinely don't understand, so make sure to try the homework in advance. Another bonus: these are on Canvas and she doesn't require you to go buy or use some alternate (and often hard to use) homework platform. Her lecture guides are the best. You can follow along with what she's teaching without having to rush to write every tiny detail on your own—I wish I had this for other classes too. With more difficult areas of ochem, she provides past lecture videos so you can hear things a second time. Her lecture notes are also scanned and uploaded. She genuinely has so many resources for you to succeed, just make sure you are taking advantage of them and go back to your notes if you have a question/approach her! She has a charismatic personality that makes lecture fun and even entertaining at times. Without her teaching, I would've enjoyed this subject a lot less. You can also tell that she loves to teach, which is something that is reflected in how many resources she has for us to succeed.

Addressing other comments: 1) she does spend time in lecture making sure people's questions are answered, and many times people's questions will be on very basic concepts. That does not mean that she is trying to spend time answering basic concepts, just that she's responding to questions. 2) As for the curve, it was honestly pretty generous. Based on exam performance, since final exam cutoffs aren't released (as is standard for chemistry), low 80s are usually an A or A-. 3) The lecture examples often reflected basic ideas because we were learning them for the first time. Make sure to go over the notes, but don't rely on these as your sole source of studying, there are practice problem sets for a reason. The exam matches the difficulty of the practice problem sets too. 

Additional comments: GSS leaders were so helpful. The ones this semester, Alice and Aubrey, were great. Make sure you try going, and even if you don't, the worksheets are provided to try (and you should do them for extra practice!!). But still, try going in person because they explain things so well. Also, study in advance. Try to keep up with content in advance of the exam because the course will go by fast (she tries to keep time for review days). Concepts in organic chemistry can become very difficult and build on each other, so getting down the basics more than a few days before the exam is important. That way, you can leave more complicated ideas for reviewing closer to the exam and ask Dr. Hirschauer about it. She also is willing to meet outside of regular office hour timings, and she's helpful.

I get that her exams have been harder this semester and that's not what people were expecting. They are difficult, and I won't deny that. However, they are not unreasonable at all. Everything you need to do well on exams is provided. Every question can be traced back to something she specifically discussed.

I have no clue what anyone means when they say Stocker is passive aggressive. She is incredibly patient with even the dumbest questions. I wouldn't say her class is fast paced, its tightly structured but she definitely gives each topic ample time. 
Orgo is a dense course so sometimes she doesn't iterate on every single minute detail and you have to fill in those gaps yourself, but the amount you have to think through yourself is very reasonable. She tells you exactly what's going to be on the exam. If she teaches something, you need to know it. The exams exclusively cover what she covers in lecture. She gives you past exams to practice with and they're very very useful for getting a grasp on how the content will be tested. The exams are very reasonable, just be careful about making silly mistakes, those losses accumulate. There are also practice problem sets on every single topic, they're a great resource. 
Orgo is a dense course and there are things you just have to memorize - but the stuff you have to memorize is generally very helpful to know and there's not a ridiculous of amount of it. 
The TA this semester (Vince) was great but I had Stocker last semester for gen-chem and the TA was just okay. If the TA is great, make use of their services. Vince was very approachable and quickly responded to emails. Shout out Vince. 
Your grade is exclusively made up of the exams, but there is a pretty nice curve. The syllabus says its 85% = A, but its usually closer to 80% = A since the averages are low. You can get around a 50% and still get a C most of the time.

My biggest tip: when Stocker says you have to memorize something, memorize it as soon as possible. It makes life alot easier.  
The one drawback is that she doesn't record lectures. If you don't plan on coming to lecture or will foreseeably miss many, then don't take Stocker.

Pros:
- Stocker explains topics very well.
- Her exams are pretty fair for the most part. As a previous review stated, DO THE PROBLEM SETS AND PRACTICE EXAMS! Her exams are very similar to them and if you want an A in this class this is a must. You should also go to office hours if you have any questions.
- Very organized in terms of giving out lots of practice problems. However, sometimes she only gives out 2 practice exams for certain exams.
- Curve is decent. As others have mentioned the minimum curve is ~5% (A range from beginning of semester is 100-85%).

Cons:
- Sometimes her classes are really fast paced, so even though she explains the topics well it takes some extra self-studying after class to fully digest them.
- She does not record her lectures or post her annotations, so you have to come to class or rely on a friend to give you the notes.
- She does not answer her emails. I ended up having to rely on emailing the TA to ask questions (Thank you Vincent!).
- Your grade is only dependent on the exams themselves. There are no other grades.

Most reviews for Dr. Koppel are for the lab section which is heavily dependent on the TA that you receive. Dr. Koppel herself however is a really sweet lady and a great lecturer. She was helpful in office hours and after lectures and made sure to always answer everyone's questions. Her lecture notes can be a little hard to follow sometimes but they're pretty good for the most part. She gives a lot of spare practice problems online and even has a whole series of recorded lectures that she uploads for each type of reaction which were super helpful. The exams for her class are pretty tough, with the average being in the low 60s. This means that around a 76-80% would earn you an A with the curve she applies. The homework is always due the night before the exam online through Achieve. It's tedious and takes a while but its online and as long as you score above an 80% of the total points you'll earn a 100% for homework credit.  She also had 10 points of extra credit which you could get through watching short animations/lectures on Achieve. I ended with an 82.48 and got an A- in the class. Overall, I'd definitely recommend Dr. Koppel.

Don't listen to the salty haters. Dixon makes you put in the work cause that's the only way you learn. She posts her notes, has prerecorded videos on the lecture, CANs, discussions packets with every problem imaginable, and the HWs mimic the exams. There are seriously unlimited resources to succeed as long as you have the time. AND she actually responds to emails unlike another chem professor I had for organic 1... In my opinion, Stocker does the bare minimum. Dixon goes above and beyond for her students BUT won't spoon-feed you the answers. Enjoyed this class and learned a lot!

Dr. Dixon is the best professor I've had at UMD so far. As long as you're keeping up, her lectures make sense and are digestible. Even on hard topics, she posts videos in the lecture folders that go over that same topic again, as well as examples. Her CAN every week is also extremely helpful, and it literally mimics whatever assignment we have due that week (homework or extra credit). Her office hours are extremely helpful. I would sit at her desk during office hours and work through the homework or the extra credit by myself or with other people, and if I was confused about something, I would just ask her right there. Discussion is also EXTREMELY helpful. Lily (the TA) usually provides a worksheet a week to cover whatever topic that week is focusing on, and the week before a midterm, she will provide an exam review. She's the GOAT. Lily will also help you with any homework or extra credit questions you have.

I've had Dr. Dixon for both Gen chem and Orgo now, and if she were teaching Orgo 2, I would've DEFINITELY taken it with her. You will have to dedicate a lot of time to this class, there are a lot of resources to help you, discussion, CAN, GSS, the videos, office hours, etc. It wasn't easy, however, it was certainly doable (and even fun with some of the jokes Dr. Dixon would make during class).

To preface, I had Dr. Dixon for both gen chem 1 and orgo 1 so this kind of a review of both but more so of orgo 1. Taking Dr. Dixon for orgo 1 after having her for gen chem 1 was the best decision I could've made. I was on the fence for a while because I knew how difficult and time consuming her home works were in gen chem and knew she could be a bit passive aggressive. But let me say orgo has been sooo much better than gen chem and Dr. Dixon is so much better at teaching orgo. Her home works for this class were so much easier I actually got them done in one sitting the day it was due which I could NEVER do in gen chem and I got an A on almost all of them. Also one homework is dropped. I never went to her office hours for orgo because in my opinion they were never helpful in gen chem, it's probably more helpful to talk with friends and ask them questions. I also never went to gss and went all the time last semester yet this class was much easier. Her exams are very fair and she has an extra credit quiz for each one which can earn you up to 12 points on the exam. I'm not gonna lie those quizzes were difficult so definitely work with others but if you can do that, you can do anything. There is no extra credit quiz for the final but she throws in some extra credit in the exam. All of the midterms have about 115 points but if you get 100/115 that's 100% on the exam. Also an A in the class is an 85% of all the points. There's also a duck race at the end of the semester which gives you 5 extra credit points. My advice is to watch all the CAN videos, which she records and posts, and watch all of her videos she posts in her lecture folders, they are both super helpful and will probably answer a lot of your questions. Overall, Dixon is very fair and offers a lot of extra credit and she can be funny too. Yes she can be a bit passive aggressive sometimes but like I said you're better off asking classmates for help than going to her office hours. If you took her for gen chem and are debating taking her for orgo 1 just take her cause you'll already be used to her teaching style and she is so much better for this class. Thank you queen Dixon for this past year in chem, it's been a pleasure doing business with you.

I would say Stocker is a very very fair professor. She gives you a ton of practice, do all of it. I enjoyed her lectures a lot and she's great at explaining things, though she does move a little fast. My one problem with her is that she provides no cushion for your grade, it only comes down to exams which sucks. Overall her class is very difficult, but if you put in the work you should get a good grade.

Take her!!! She teaches in a very organized, easy to follow way, and keeps lecture interesting. As someone who learns from examples, she offers so much practice: test-like example problems in class, worksheets on cavas, late night problem-solving zoom session, and any other type you request if you visit her during office hours. Her exams are very predictable and very fair-- it will never be something you have not seen before. Yes-- all of the orgo professors are good, but when comparing her to the others (who my friends took) her organization of content made more sense to me (and she has a nice curve AND homework to help!). As far as exams, it is very possible to get an A, even above-- there is extra credit! When looking at grades, they seem to be mostly determined by how much you study. The best advice I can give for Koppel is: study content as you get taught it in lecture, go to her late night zooms (test questions directly from!), study in advance so that if you are slightly confused on anything-- office hours!
The curve is insane, just practice hard and you will be fine.

(Fall 2024)
Amazing, approachable professor and very engaging lecturer. I loved her teaching style, especially having Stocker the semester after. She's really nice, and has moments to breathe and practice problems built into her lectures. Her lecture guides were easy to follow along, and she posted her annotations in case you missed something. It wasn't everything that she covered, and sometimes were incomplete. She's also totally fine if you come ask her questions outside of office hours. If she's in her office and the door is open, she will absolutely take questions. I practically abused this when I had her for orgo 2 lab and it saved my ass so many times.

Pros:
- Class was curved so the average became the B-/C+ cutoff. Her exams always felt fair, and the 10% HW with 8 attempts was a nice grade boost that was practically free, and did genuinely help me to understand material better.
- Lecture guides to follow along, copying mechanisms and things becomes less of a hassle that way
- Posts actual lecture notes
- Moments to breathe built into lectures, along with practice problems in lecture
- Answers (and asks!) questions during lectures to check for understanding
- Her practice problems feel like exam problems, (maybe slightly easier?)
- Very approachable! Both through email and outside of office hours. Seriously, just show up.

Cons:
- No practice exams posted
- Not all content talked about is in the lecture notes (this shouldn't be a problem if you pay attention during lecture tbh)
- HW is graded a little confusingly for multiple-answer questions (but also she explains this and you get 8 attempts)

I wanted to take Hirschauer, like everyone else who probably ended up in Stocker's class. Stocker is a fantastic lecturer, don't get me wrong, but she goes way too fast. I needed to record her lectures to understand what she went over in class that day. However, I fell into the trap of using all my time to go over lectures instead of doing practice. 

Like everyone else said, the practice that she gives is very helpful and genuinely representative of the type of problems that you'll encounter on the exams. I'm an idiot, and I barely did any practice prior to the exams, relying on the fact that I had a solid grasp of the theory. Don't be like me, I don't understand what was going through my head. I didn't do so hot on the midterms, but when it came to the finals and I had time to dedicate to solely orgo, I did all the practice and had a "oh shoot, nothing was ever that difficult" sort of epiphany, and I clutched up on the final. 

I just have an awful work ethic, not gonna lie. You need to be locked in constantly if you're going to take Stocker. Stay on top of practice and stay on top of understanding all of the content and theory. My two labs fell during her office hours, so I never could go, and then I had another class immediately after lecture, so I couldn't stay after class to ask questions. I'd recommend switching around your schedule so that you can prioritize going to office hours and staying after class for questions. 

Overall, a very doable class, but you'll need to have a good work ethic throughout the entire semester and be prepared to spend lots of time on this class if you want an A. Lowkey contemplating using freshman forgiveness because I know for a fact that I could've done better in her class if I were smarter about studying this semester.

I hate her exams. Her pp sets are nothing like the exams, and I feel like I spent HOURS studying just for her to pull crazy stuff out last minute. honestly i studied the most for her final and she said it was "30, 30, 40" in terms of the breakdown for units but that WHOLE THING was basically nmr and unit 3 so.... i feel like i knew the content it was just that her exams were always a curveball and i wanted to cry during them

Her HW was so free (automatic 100% on all because you had 8 attempts, so they were a grade booster)! Yet, her exams were HARD. The most annoying part about it was that she didn't give you any practice exams to study from, so you were basically going in blind. The only thing you had were her PP sets (which were relatively not the same difficulty level as her exams). With that being said, I loved the structure of her course. She posted lecture guides that you could download to your iPad and write on while following along in class. This made sure that I wasn't cramming to take down notes and was actually able to understand what she was lecturing about. However, she does tend to go fast in her lectures, so just keep that in mind. I have always heard that professors who teach big courses like this don't provide enough opportunities to help students, and they don't care about you, but I was glad to learn that Hirschauer was not like this. Her doors were always open, and she would help you during office hours. She was very warm-hearted and it's obvious she's passionate about what she teaches & genuinely wants you to succeed. Her exams are hard though and not as easy as people in the past have said they were. 
Orgo is definitely a course that you need to spend time with. You CANNOT just study for the exam a few days before (you need to have a plan & actually start studying even 2 weeks before). I find it best to go over the concepts after we learn them, that way by the time exam prep comes around, you're reviewing the information you already know rather than trying to learn it. I think you can succeed in this class if you try hard enough and put in the effort. Just to give you some clarity: I ended with an 80% and got an A-, so even if you feel like you're failing, just lock in and you can do it!

Although Dr. Stocker says that she is an organic chemist, she isn't necessarily the best at explaining how exactly you are supposed to do it.  Let me tell you, orgo has to do with so many reactions that you have to have memorized.  You NEED to become familiar with them as soon as possible, in addition to showing the mechanisms and how to perform them.  I had to get a tutor to help me to pass this class because GSS personally was extremely unhelpful and felt like a waste of my time.  They would go over information that was irrelevant to the lecture given that day, as the GSS leaders did not attend our classes.  The first exam was extremely difficult for the entire class, as most people received D's.  The second exam was primarily focused on alkene reactions and was a bit better with ranges within the B to C range.  The very last midterm was the most difficult with the range falling with 64% = B.  The final was very fair, however she put a question on the exam that she said she would not put again, because when she had it on the last midterm everyone ended up getting a 0 on it.  I took her for gen chem and thought it would be better with Stocker, but very likely it may have been better to take this class with Hirschauer.  Lastly, the overall grade curve was very heavy and we did not have any HW, so grades overall relied HEAVILY on midterms and the final exam.

Dr. Stocker is an amazing orgo professor. She is a great lecturer and makes class very fun and engaging. She explains things very clearly and uses fun examples and analogies to explain different concepts, which makes a difficult subject like orgo more approachable and enjoyable. I was nervous when I found out grades were solely based on exams; however, Dr. Stocker provides A LOT of practice materials. She provides 4 ungraded homework assignments with the answer keys and multiple old exams (she will usually only post answer keys for 2 of the old exams). She also provides a problem set for almost every single concept covered in class, which was SUPER helpful. You really have to utilize all her practice materials to do well because a lot of similar questions show up on the tests. Her exams were fair and usually only contained material we reviewed and practiced in class. Dr. Stocker was also very kind and approachable and would always stay after class to answer any questions. Her final exam is fair, and she curves well. For reference, my average after the final was 84.67%, and it got curved to an A. Overall, you can definitely do well in Dr. Stocker's class; it just takes hard work and practice. Orgo is not an easy subject, but I feel that taking it with Dr. Stocker made it more simple and fun. 
Also, shoutout to our TA, Vince, who was super helpful. He reviewed everything we covered in lectures in discussion and went over multiple problems and examples. He would always encourage us to email him with questions and would usually answer the emails very promptly. 

Good Luck in Orgo! You got this ; )

If you took Friedman, Dr. Koppel will feel like a lifesaver. I nearly failed General Chemistry, but with Dr. Koppel for Organic Chemistry, I got an A.

I loved her class. She explains things clearly and gets straight to the point. Honestly, I love her teaching style—though my only comparison is Friedman. She's very straightforward and will tell you exactly what you need to know and what you don’t.

For example, if she thinks a topic isn’t worth stressing over (like nomenclature), she won’t overemphasize it. That part was like 10 points on Midterm 1 and never showed up again.

She thoroughly explains concepts in a way that makes sense if you’re paying attention. Her exams are fair and similar to the practice problems she gives—she provides lots of practice.

If she’s still teaching lab, she connects it to what you’re doing in class, which helps a lot. (side note about lab: go to office hours IT WILL SAVE YOUR GRADE, but find the ones that are actually helpful). A lot of people struggle with mechanisms, but those of us who had Koppel at least understood the basics, especially for lab concepts like radicals. And if you need more help in her class, she provides supplemental videos in the lab that can be used in lecture portions.

That’s just my experience, though. Some people feel she goes too fast, but I haven’t heard many complaints about the difficulty of her exams. Honestly, it’s one of those “you either get it or you don’t” situations—but that applies to any professor 😭

Some notes on Professor Koppel and my experience:
- I didn’t go to office hours or ask questions in class, but I did sit in the front.
- I started studying several days in advance using YouTube videos, one-pagers, practice problems, and flashcards. I didn’t really use the textbook.
- The homework setup is a bit unusual — you have until each midterm to complete the corresponding sets. You only need about 80% for full credit. I 
      mostly used the homework to study the week before each exam.
- Her exams are very fair. If you do the practice exams, you’ll be well prepared. The final was long but also fair.
- For mechanisms, use flashcards and practice them repeatedly.
- Go to all the late-night review sessions and practice exams — they help a lot.
- She seems funny and nice; she often cracks jokes during class.
- My TA was also really helpful in explaining things.

Lecture notes are top-notch.
Lots of work, but a very enjoyable class. I made great friends in it.
Homework is helpful, PP sets are helpful. ( I did each one three times over, once to grasp, once before the exam, and once before the final.)
A wonderful person--very nice and a great sense of humor.
One of my favorite professors.

Hey everyone,

After reading some of the reviews here, I felt like I needed to share my experience. I took Organic Chemistry with Dr. H in the spring and ended up withdrawing. I thought I could “figure it out,” but that approach did not work for me. When I retook the course with Dr. H the following semester, everything changed. She genuinely believed in me and emphasized that success would come with consistent practice.

I didn’t do anything over winter break to prepare, yet I ended up with an A- that semester. Honeslty, the difference was that I did orgo every single day. Dr. H’s exams are fair—they test whether you understand the concepts, not your ability to memorize random material. She never includes topics that haven’t been discussed in class. Chemistry is hard (I was in tears y'all), but blaming the exams isn’t fair—they are designed to reflect your understanding, and that’s exactly what she evaluates.

I also went to office hours a few times for extra help, and she was incredibly supportive. Sure, sometimes I couldn’t grasp certain concepts right away, but she still guided me and pushed me to understand the material. Not every interaction will be great, but you get what you put into it. Honestly, I absolutely love Dr. H and would take CHEM 231 with her a million times over. 

Regardless of who you take you're going to have to work your butt off--that's just orgo for you. So, as long as you can explain why the heck you're drawing that arrow there you'll be fine :)
Nice but moves very fast

Good teacher, very nice -> first time teaching the class collectively but is genuine and cares for his students to succeed. Not sure about curves right now but the way he's teaching it makes a lot more sense (coming from a person retaking Chem 231 -> f*ck Dixon). He tends to go a little fast and past lecture time but it's not the end of the world. You also get plenty of resources.

As a person, she is very sweet and she cares a lot about her students. As a professor, she can be kind of hard to follow and unorganized. I think this more so had to do with the course and the difficulty of the content. I believe she is probably one of the better options for orgo, but in all honesty we can all agree there really isn't a "good" option in the umd chemistry department.

I already wrote a review for her but I realized I left out a very important con of taking her: her notes are actually awful. She basically just scribbles down random structures and then uploads them on canvas so if you miss class you're screwed. She also has really bad handwriting that I have trouble reading even though I have bad handwriting.

I am honestly surprised by the other reviews I have seen of Dr. Hong so far. He talks extremely quietly and fast in lecture. There have been multiple times when students have to raise their hands and ask him to either speak up or slow down (this happens at least once a lecture). A TA of this class told us to actually stop taking notes because it is impossible to keep up and understand at the same time. I have had to teach myself every topic in this class through tutoring and YouTube videos. Dr. Hong does not record his lectures and only posts the notes which he writes as he goes during the lecture making them often confusing. His weekly homework worksheets are very difficult and are on the same level of difficulty as the exams. There is extra credit on each exam, but the questions make no sense and are usually unrelated to the topic (ex. He will ask about a random Nobel Prize winner) while the other classes had simple extra credit like “what did you dress up as for Halloween?” I usually do not get any of the extra credit and neither does anyone else I know taking the course with Hong. He also does the curve based off class average, so the curve is not as big as the other classes. Right now, an 87 is an A in our class whereas other classes have an 80 as the A which seems unfair due to the difficulty of the subject. Organic Chemistry is a difficult subject no matter what, but I did not feel prepared for it from the lectures with Dr. Hong. No student should have to entirely teach themselves a class of this level of difficulty.

DO NOT TAKE DR. HONG. As soon as you enter the class, he treats you like youre a breaking-bad fanatic and know the ins and outs of orgo. The only upside is that his worksheets occasionally have practice problems that show up on the exam. Otherwise, he speeds through notes in class, ALWAYS goes overtime, is disorganized with notes that are hard to follow if you happen to miss class, and refuses to post certain resources on canvas. At the beginning of the semester, he said he was going to teach the course like it was a "summer class," forcing us to rush through topics and be ahead of every other Orgo 1 lecture by 1-2 weeks. The one day we had a different orgo 1 professor sub our lecture was the only day content made sense. The only way to possibly succeed in his class is if you are retaking Orgo 1 and already generally know the info of the class before walking in. If you can take another professor or hop on the waitlist, do it.

Dr. Hirschauer is an amazing lecturer. I had her 50 minute 3x a week class and I left every lecture having some grasp on the material. She makes her lectures relatively easy to follow and really gets to the point when it comes to learning topics. Anything that is not needed she really will not make you learn so everything fits together well which makes it easier to follow. Her exams this semester were very fair, we have not had the final yet but I can only hope it is the same. The only kind of negative is that Dr. Hirschauer can be a little blunt during office hours, she is very helpful but will call you out for not knowing something especially if it is close to the exam date which can be a little off putting. She also can come off a bit judgmental if you ask her a question that she expects you to know the answer to. Her homeworks were really easy to get 100 on and she gives a lot of resources for exams that help A LOT. I highly recommend taking her for orgo 1.

Whatever you do, DO NOT take Dr. HONG for Orgo 1. He is the WORST teacher I have ever had at UMD. A lot of people trash talk him but I really liked Dr.Hong. It was his first semester teaching orgo and I think he did great. I feel like if you go to lecture, do the homework (easy 5 points just for completion), and study using his practice exams along with some YouTube videos, there's almost no way for you to fail the course. No chemistry class will be an easy A but if you put in the work, taking Hong won't be bad.

I'm back yet again to review my queen... I took her in CHEM131 for freshman connection and continued to take her for CHEM231. I will say, Orgo 1 was more work and much more learning than Chem 131, in my opinion. However, because it's all relatively new information, you can start orgo with a blank slate and not be weighed down if you got a bad score in gen chem. The only real thing that transferred over was electronegativity. Moreover, if you pay attention to her lectures, you will 110% never need to open a textbook or watch a YouTube video: her lectures are THAT thorough and helpful. 

I will repeat what I said for CHEM131 with her: if you are premed or are genuinely interested in grasping the material, PLEASE take her. 
I am currently taking Orgo 2 under another professor, and JUST USING Dixon's Orgo 1 knowledge, I can maintain a 97% with VERY MINIMAL studying. I literally cried at the beginning of this semester because I realized how much better of a lecturer she is than most other chemistry professors at this uni, and I would need to wait for another year or so to take biochemistry with her. 

Those who have been leaving one-star reviews just sound hella salty about their skill issues. i think dr. hirschauer's the goat!!! imma try to give as comprehensive of a breakdown as i can without getting bored and giving up on this review so bear with me please:

exam 1 (on a monday i think): very representative of her problem sets. no surprises, nothing like that. i think acid/base was on this exam, so for that, i recommend using flashcards to memorize the functional groups + their pKas (she's so nice for having us memorize rounded pKas rather than the more accurate decimal) and then after you've got those down, search up a random medication/drug molecular formula image on google to see if you can identify the functional groups and their pKas (i credit the second recommendation to aubrey from gss lol).

exam 2 (on a wed): iiiii didn't like this exam, not because it wasn't representative, but because this was personally my worst exam + this is when you really start learning orgo stuff according to her and praha (the ta). i distinctly remember praha telling us this exam is like 5 times harder than exam 1 (but don't let that scare you!! just overcompensate by studying more yessir). to this day, i hate substitution and elimination reactions (i only started feeling good about them during office hours held right before we took the exam), and stereochem is a little rough. looking back at my mistakes, though, a lot of them were kind of stupid or minor and those added up - it wasn't like i completely blanked on a whole question though.

exam 3 (on a wed): technically this is the worst exam content-wise and tbh everything-wise... BUT no curveball questions imo. she curved this exam itself rather than adjusting the overall course curve (i think that's how it worked??). i uh studied for ~5 hours per day for the five days before the exam though and did maybe an hour per day of alkene reaction practice for the week or two before that. this unit genuinely sucks to learn though because you have to memorize what 14?? alkene reactions and a handful more alkyne reactions and yk... sometimes it feels like "what's the point in doing all of this" because dr. h would straight up say in class "yeah you kinda have to just memorize this stuff." for this unit, i recommend making your own summary sheet for all of the reactions, stating their name, mechanism (i tried to find patterns in these - e.g. three membered ring), anti/syn addition, markovnikov/anti-markovnikov addition, racemic product, etc. i thought her starter + challenge sets were great for mastering these b/c they literally just had you do each reaction with each molecule given.

final: this one.. was kinda hard. not the worst, not the best. weird thing is my confidence level was similar to my exam 2 confidence, but i actually did well. unfortunately, i didn't go back to see my exam so i don't have much... ask dr. h for a breakdown on how much of each exam's content is on the final tho. for us it was like approximately exam 1: 20%, exam 2: 32%, exam 3: 32%, post-exam 3 (nmr): 20% or something i don't remember.

other nice details about exams:
- she has maybe like 5 ish? extra credit points on each exam which is nice - they're not all free per se, but they're not extremely hard at least.
- exams usually get graded and grades posted within 2-3 days.
- you can get your midterms back during discussion and keep them. for the final, she just announces a time for people to come view it - no pictures, no taking it home.

grade cutoffs: dr. h posts an announcement with overall course grade cutoffs after each exam + stats like median for the exam + course. grade cutoffs tell you what the minus mark is (e.g. after exam 3 for us, an 86 was an a-, but we didn't know what an a was). note that for the final, she doesn't release grade cutoffs so no one ever knows how much you need at that point :( that made me stress quite a bit... welp. it's prob that the curve gets bigger though from what people say.

homework: an elms quiz per week - 8 attempts per quiz. she says due saturday, but they're lowkey due sunday night to account for tech difficulties - just get it out of the way early though so that if you use up some attempts, you have time to ask her for help or at least to work at it some more. multiple select is annoying, but i won't complain because 8 attempts is beautiful. def possible to get 100% on all of them eventually even if some are a little harder.

dr. hirschauer herself: really nice and funny! not as unhinged of a sense of humor as dr. hong, but she makes us laugh. tries her best to answer questions during lecture but sometimes can't. wish she could do more practice problems during lecture with us... but it's a time crunch with the syllabus. thus also goes kinda fast sometimes. she's really trying to convince the chem department to let her keep recording lectures with panopto, so please attend lectures or else you're just proving the dept right! her recordings are awesome for quick re-learning on your own when you feel like you're falling behind, esp during exam 2 and 3 content.

our ta, praha: soooo a lot of people don't like him. but i do. whoops. he's kind of blunt/passive aggressive about stuff, but i think it's a good reality check... even if he tells us we didn't do as well on an exam as he'd expected since the exam was easier than normal... anyway he holds office hrs on zoom before each exam

how to study:
- do her problem sets for each chapter. starter sets and challenge sets too if she makes those available. if you can do those pretty solidly, you're in good shape. prob better if you work on them as she goes over the content in lecture - i started getting behind and would do them the week or two before the exam. some people ik would redo them before exams on top of that.
- go to her office hours! if you can't make her normal time, shoot her an email the minute you find out (just get it out of the way at the start of the sem) saying you have a conflict and ask if she has any other availability. her office hours can get really full when you get to the week of or before the exam - i remember there were like 7 people in her office and maybe 7 more lined up outside before the final. nice thing is: she hosts extra office hours before each exam to give people more chances to ask questions. there's also a nice table outside her and dr. koppel's offices with a whiteboard where a lot of us would hang out and work on problems until we had a question for her. sometimes she'd come out of her office to help us there but only if there were a LOT of people.
- ask questions during lecture if they come up or go up to her right after lecture ends. keeping a list of questions in my notes app helped me remember them all. might also help to sit closer to the front imo (i say this lightly but it is a STRONG recommendation if you get shy asking questions like i do).
- go to gss sessions with alice and/or aubrey. i personally loved aubrey's worksheets (they were just cute okay -_-), but some people said alice posts harder problems. i honestly slacked off on attending these halfway through the semester, but i still kept doing the worksheets on my own since they're posted on elms. they have review sessions too, but i also uh never attended any except for the final due to schedule conflicts. the final review session was lowkey messy cuz they made mistakes, but they are usually quite good so let's cut them some slack yeah. go gss!!
- praha's discussion worksheets are nice even if i didn't use them consistently - i recommend attending discussion cuz he's very straightforward about recommended studying tips + it's a more closer-knit setting to ask questions and he has more time to dive into the why of the chemistry that we're doing.
- go to chem department problem solving sessions! this sem they were online via zoom thursday nights (9-10 pm). i got some nice tidbits from those - like what a nitro group looks like - and it's good to get extra practice + advice from different profs (the orgo profs take turns hosting these sessions). i also think if i went to the last one on nmr spectroscopy maybe i would've understood it better haha but it worked out okay for me.
- get the organic chemistry as a second language book (first semester) by david klein - there's a free pdf online (alice and aubrey linked it on the gss page on elms) or you can get the physical copy (i liked the physical cuz it's a workbook so i could solve problems in it). nice supplementary material after you're done with dr. h's stuff or if you want to get ahead and preview content for future lectures. note that the first semester book does not cover ir/nmr/ms spectroscopy (that's in the second sem book) + doesn't have the oxymercuration/demercuration alkene reaction. might be missing a few other things, but honestly solid practice material.

I would also suggest going to the GSS, those are very useful. 

With that being said, he does go FAST. He goes incredibly fast, and sometimes it is hard to keep up with him during lecture. I do find myself watching organic chemistry tutor at times due to his speed. However, he is always open to answering questions, especially during his lectures. Just make sure not to fall behind because he doesn't record lectures.

If you get stressed easily by professors that have a disorganized way of teaching Dr.Koppel is not the teacher for you. She begins each topic with the general ideas and then focuses in on smaller topics but there are no order or outlines to follow. Looking back over my notes was a nightmare and if you miss a class and look at her posted notes, you will be beyond confused. I highly recommend the Orgo as a second language books if taking this course. 
The curve is based off of class average which was decently high for my class but I passed with a C with a 58 somehow.
The online quizzes and assignments boost your grade but the exams and TLQ in lab are challenging and she does not give you any type of review and will usually be 1/3 of the way through new material, before the exam which gets hard to manage.
If you dedicate the time and are good at self-teaching she's not a bad teacher but you cannot slack off or have a bad week you will fall behind orgo is alot of material!
She’s a a little intimidating but a really good teacher. I learned a lot and would definitely recommend her!

Take this professor. I attended GSS weekly and did the practice exams, and I was always well above the average on the exams. Lecture can be a little confusing at times if you don't review the material beforehand, but as long as you keep up with the content, you will be fine. I would definitely recommend taking Koppel! - I thought her exams were fair, and the curve is very generous. She offers Zooms at night with extra practice problems before every midterm and will answer questions. She clearly cares about her students a lot and keeps lecture interesting. Most of these bad reviews are for lab, which was a different story and unavoidable... I still did well in it, but found it to be even harder than lecture. Make sure to go to the TAs with questions, and they can help you out.

imo Dr. Hong is a great professor and I'd recommend him highly. He explains things well, puts effort into making lectures interesting/entertaining, clearly cares about the students, and is just a chill guy. 

Some folks blame him for speeding through content - that's fair, but I feel like it's not his fault. OChem is just a hard class with a lot of material to pack into one semester. Going to class is not gonna be enough; no matter how good the professor is, you gotta familiarize yourself with the material on your own. Besides, I'd rather get through all the material a bit faster and have some time for review than be scrambling close to finals because we didn't cover the last couple topics in time. 

To his credit, Dr. Hong gives a LOT of practice material: between weekly homeworks, practice exams, past exams, past discussion worksheets, etc. (all can be found in ELMS), he makes sure students have many chances to grapple with material and really lock the concepts down outside of lecture. I know it's tedious but you should do that extra practice, it will be a huge help. (also, Dr. Hong seems to like reusing questions from practice worksheets/tests to reward you if you did them :D ) 
I should also mention that his TA / GSS leaders (Dennis / Ariana & Sophia) are super nice and helpful, I'd definitely recommend going to discussions / GSS if you want help with a particular topic, have questions about the material, or just want even more practice. 

Exams are not easy but they are definitely fair. Usually there'll be a few tricky questions but nothing egregious. He also emails a list of exam topics before every exam, so if you just follow that you should be good. 
I'd recommend going to all his lectures (as aforementioned I think he explains things clearly and thoroughly, plus he sometimes gives hints for bonus points) and sit in the front rows if you can (so you can hear him better, and so you can participate). 

TLDR: Dr. Hong is a very solid professor and a lovely person as well. If you lock in for lectures and use the resources he and his TAs provide, you'll definitely do great in his class.

That being said though, your grade is heavily weighted on exams. She provided NO help for studying for her exams which mind you WERE THE WORST. She would say to do the practice problems that were wayyy easier than the exam, I would study for hours after class for her exams and it was just a waste of time and stress because the exam would be completely different than what you think it would be. If you are a good test taker go ahead and take her but if you are not and think studying for hours wasting your time will help, it won't so save yourself and don't take her if you're bad at taking exams/have test anxiety. I took Dr. Hong in Fall 25 which was his first semester as a professor. 

Pros:
- Weekly homework graded on completion (put down pretty much anything).
- Fair exams with similar questions to the discussion worksheets. The final exam had large sections that were directly pulled from the midterms.
- Posts his notes which were generally in-depth and helpful for studying.
- Great curve, I had an 88% and ended up with an A. This will of course depend on how your cohort does though.

Cons:
- I did not like his lecture style at all. I never felt as though concepts were being explained and it sometimes seemed like he was talking more to himself while writing on his iPad (sit at the front as he does not project).
- The practice exams were not particularly helpful as they were not similar to the actual exams, however this may change if he posts the exams we took for later semesters.

Overall I'd recommend Hong. Do the discussion worksheets, go to the GSS exam review sessions if you can, and maybe watch some Crash Course Organic Chemistry. Good luck!

take her! there's a lot of good about this class, but I think what stood out to me was her love for the subject that she brought to class every single day (despite all the complaining/lazy/inattentive/grade-grubbing undergrads she had/has to deal with, which i find seriously impressive), be it building a cohesive narrative/thoroughly motivating the various topics we covered as we moved throughout the course, telling stories of past experiment woes, giving real-life context to certain reactions (eg this reaction is regularly used in industry for xyz, if I was doing this in lab I'd probably change this, etc), offering ideas for different ways we could earn a Nobel prize, etc. i think you get the idea. 

not only were her lectures super engaging, she also just seemed to 'get' how someone new to organic chemistry might struggle (which I did), and taught with that in mind. I've since forgotten what exactly the subject was, but I remember we were discussing a reaction with an unexpected product, and after stepping through one example, she said something along the lines of "let's try xyz, maybe it'll be better [it didn't]". maybe not the most compelling example, but it really resonated with me, as I can't think of many other professors I've had that came with that perspective. Her willingness to abuse notation/skip on some formalism for our understanding also went hard af.

other pros:
- she provide plenty of resources to help you succeed in the class (as the below reviews have covered, eg the late night show, past exams, creating fresh practice problems to supplement exam prep, etc)
- homework is graded on an adjusted scale, with 80% correct being an A
- straightforward exams, interesting extra credit problems occasionally. what she covers in lecture is what's tested, there's generally no curveballs, and regrades for TA errors were prompt
- good textbook. you get lifetime digital access, it's the same text used in CHEM242, and the text is super straightforward/teaches you what you need to know. would HIGHLY recommend paying the addl $10 for the included practice problems/key. 
- posts her notes to ELMS as a PDF

cons (minor)
- lecture not recorded
- $30 for Wiley e-text (but wtv, she also offers a FOSS alternative text, it just has a less 1-1 correspondence with lecture topics. reading guide is provided to match though)


in summary, 10/10 no notes please do yourself a favor and take her class
